creates.title: Four Thousand Weeks: Time Management for Mortals
creates.author: Oliver Burkeman
creates.review:
"In the long run, we're all dead."

The best thing about this book was its title. This entire book could be summed up in just a few sentences—not sure why Burkeman decided to have us waste precious time with all his waffling and unnecessary anecdotes ... instead of saving us some time, ha.

In reality, it all boils down to just the title: we are mortal! We will NEVER have enough time to do everything we want to do. So might as well just prioritize and enjoy life while you can.

---------------------------------------------

"I soon discovered that when you get tremendously efficient at answering email, all that happens is that you get much more email."

"This notion that fulfillment might lie in embracing, rather than denying, our temporal limitations wouldn't have surprised the philosophers of ancient Greece and Rome. The noblest of human goals wasn't to become godlike, but to wholeheartedly human instead."

"Work expands so as to fill the time available for its completion."

"What you pay attention to will define, for you, what reality is."

"The human disease is often painful, but it's only unbearable for long as you are under the impression that there might be a cure. Accept the inevitability of the affliction, and freedom ensues."

"Death may be the enemy, but it is also the natural order of things."

This book was gold—a much-needed reminder that we are all mortal. It might seem morbid to dwell on death, to obsess about the way people age ... but I found the topic to be refreshing, and even motivating, because of how jarring it is. Discussing the inevitability of death can feel painful, but if anything it offers a powerful perspective on how we should be treasuring our lives today. Aging is a daunting topic not brought up often in regular conversation, but Gawande makes a good case for why it should be.

This book is one of those rare instances of absolute magic that occurs when the author is fully passionate about his subject and devotes his life to the study of it. We are very lucky he decided to translate his thoughts into this well-written series of case studies. 

--------------------------------------------

"There's no escaping the tragedy of life, which is that we are all aging from the day that we are born."

"It is not death that the very old tell me they fear. It is what happens short of death—losing their hearing, their memory, their best friends, their way of life."

"The chance to shape one's story is essential to sustaining meaning in life."

Sharpen your wisdom, distinguish principle and its opposite in the world, learn the good and bad of all things, … This is the heart of the wisdom of the martial arts.

Great tips for winning warrior battles that also translate well into winning at everyday life. It makes sense why the quant company was named after this. 

---------------------------------------------

Though the mind appears weak on the surface, it should be strong on the bottom.

In fighting and in everyday life you should be determined though calm.

You will get rich by giving society what it wants but does not yet know how to get. At scale.

So funny that what originally started as a tweet storm has transformed into a book that is worth way more than its weight in gold. Naval freely reveals the exact secrets to exponential growth and true wealth creation, beyond the fallacy of earning a linear salary that will only lead to finite amounts of money. 

Rating this five stars purely because this book could transform the trajectory of a life. Understanding these concepts is like escaping the matrix of the rat race that society likes to imprison us in. 

But beyond just financial freedom, this book also includes principles on life, art, and happiness. Perhaps like a modern day Tao Te Ching ... (& it does actually pull from a lot of Buddhist philosophies)

I also appreciated the emphasis on how important reading is for a successful life. It's sad to see our society gravitating toward TikToks and Labubus when hidden gems of wisdom, past philosophies, and raison d'etre are all still waiting for us in books from the greats who lived before us.

For the sake of attention spans I'll keep this review short ... but I couldn't recommend this book more for anyone who wants to achieve financial freedom, and mental freedom, in our modern society. 

--------------------------------------------------------------------

Be the best in the world at what you do. Keep redefining what you do until this is true.

If you're not 100% into, somebody else who is 100% into it will outperform you. 

Escape competition through authenticity.

The most important skill for getting rich is becoming a perpetual learner.

Earn with your mind, not your time. 

Always pay it forward. And don't keep count.

Praise specifically, criticize generally.

A calm, a fit body, and a house full of love. These things cannot be bought. They must be earned.

Don't take yourself so seriously. You're just a monkey with a plan.

Happiness is what's there when you remove the sense that something is missing in your life.

A happy person is someone who effortlessly interprets events in such a way that they don't lose their innate peace.

If you create it for yourself, it's art. If you create it for others, it's business.

All greatness comes from suffering.

"The greatest danger is in standing still."

Four stars just because the title of this book is all you really need to read. Facts asf.

The rest of the book was full of some outdated fluff from Intel's pre-2000s rise, told from the CEO's POV. (Crazy. Before iPhones & WiFi & Airpods & TikTok and all that ...) But still a few gems of how to act as a leader, told through dated but still interesting anecdotes.

-----------------------------------------------------

"In technology, whatever can be done will be done."

"The sad news is, nobody owes you a career. Your career is literally your business. You own it as a sole proprietor."

"Businesspeople are not just managers, they are also human. They have emotions"

"Put all of your eggs in one basket, and watch that basket."

"A finite game is played for the purpose of winning, an infinite game for the purpose of continuing to play." 

Extraordinary. Such refined and logical reasoning to come to the most nonsensical yet true conclusions. It's so reassuring to hear that the most wonderful way, and the only truly logical way, of living is to approach life as an infinite game.

-------------------------------------------

"A finite game is played for the purpose of winning, an infinite game for the purpose of continuing to play." 

"To be serious is to press for a specified conclusion. To be playful is to allow for possibility whatever the cost to oneself."

"If surprise is no longer possible, all play ceases. Surprise causes finite play to end. It is the reason for infinite play to continue."

"To be prepared against surprise is to be trained. To be prepared for surprise is to be educated."

"Power is always measured in units of comparison."

"All the limits of finite play are self-limitations."

"Only that which can change can continue."

"The creative is found for anyone who is prepared for surprise."

"True creators do not display their art so as to make it appear real. They display the real in a way that reveals it to be art."

"Nature, to be commanded, must be obeyed."

"Storytelling is not combative. It does not succeed or fail. Instead of placing one body of knowledge against another, storytellers invite us to return from knowledge to thinking."

"Myths, told for their own sake, are not stories that have meanings, but stories that give meanings."

"Everything in life is a mind game."

Wow. Goggins' life story is genuinely incredible, almost to the point where it reads as unreal. He is one crazy, superhuman motherf*cker—but at the core still very much human, which is the reassuring and powerful part about this book. Although physical traits inevitably play a part, it's fascinating that Goggins achieved his life's work mainly by conditioning his mind. 

Lots of actionable life lessons from Goggins about developing a calloused mind, embracing failures, and never cutting corners. Perhaps he's like a modern day Buddha lol—a modern man who has found an unshakeable sense of inner peace. Extremely inspiring.

My one qualm is that this book is very clearly ghostwritten, and even in the audiobook version there are short "podcast" clips where the author is excessively glazing Goggins in conversation. It's ok though ... Goggins' story is so crazy that it still resonates very strongly.

------------------------------------------------------------

"Human beings change through study, habit, and stories."

"I had to be more than motivated. I had to become literally obsessed to the point where people thought I was fucking nuts."

"Always be willing to embrace your ignorance and become the dumb fuck in the classroom again, because that is the only way to expand your mind."

"Most wars are won or lost in our own heads."

"There is no finish line."

"Hard work creates opportunities."

You can tell that this man was a four-star US Navy admiral just from listening to the crisp way he enunciates his words in the audiobook. Straightlaced and disciplined, McRaven gives excellent advice that translates smoothly from the battlefield into any corporate or leadership setting. The principles themselves are a bit generic, like you would find in any leadership book, but the real world examples he gives from his time in SEAL training and in the field add color to them. If anything, it's just fascinating to learn a bit about behind-the-scenes US military operations and the sheer feats of human discipline that they require. 

"You must have a personal code of conduct that provides an anchor for your decisions and your actions."

“The day you no longer believe you have something to prove, the day you no longer believe you must give it your all, the day you think you are entitled to special treatment, the day you think all your hard days are behind you, is the day you are no longer the right leader for the job.”

"Who dares, wins. Who sweats, wins. Who plans, wins"

"Never rely on hope as a strategy."

"A shepherd should smell like his sheep."

"The harder I worked, the more luck I seemed to have."
epic. the finished-in-3-sittings type of good. will collect my thoughts after the horror at humanity’s evils has time to truly set in.

Is this book a genius masterpiece or just complete shitshow? Don't really know the answer to that, but I'm still glad I gave this a try. Perfect book for any self-respecting insane narcissistic plastic people-pleaser girlie. (guilty 🙋‍♀️)

___________

"You're too crushed and obsessed about being poor to have always been poor." 

"Things aren't always what they seem, are they."

"What good is it to be left without no trace? To be wounded, without the pleasure of a scar."

"If you can't tell the difference between reality and illusion, we can't help you. A true artist knows the difference. I remember learning that that's actually the difference between an actual artist and, like, an insane person. You know?"

"All the love and hate I have in my heart. Plus one fucking bunny."

An incredible true story, but a somewhat mediocre retelling of it. Too comfortable, too indulgent—the author never truly experienced any of the suffering in this story firsthand, and it shows. She did a fairly decent job trying her best though—and honestly an outstanding job when you take into consideration that this was her first real foray into novel writing. Still, there were parts of this book that read like teen-angst, sexually-fantasized fanfiction and I did not like that. 

It pales in comparison to much more heartfelt portrayals of the Holocaust, like Man's Search for Meaning (nonfiction) or even All the Light We Cannot See (fiction). I also did not find a single quote in this entire novel that I wanted to note down, which has not happened for the past 2 dozen books I've read this year. Probably a bad sign that, once again, this book has an amazing story behind it but just very mediocre writing to convey it.

Tedious at times but still imaginative and thought-provoking.
